title: Making a POS Legally Sellable in Belgium
subtitle: Shipping GKS 2.0 fiscal compliance across an iPad POS app and a restaurant Dashboard
summary: Built the fiscal layer that lets Onesix's POS operate legally in Belgium: FOD-exact X/Z reports, signed fiscal events, per-line refunds, money in/out, an employee PIN lock on the iPad and fiscal data on every receipt.
context:
Onesix sells a self-service Kiosk, an iPad POS app (Merchant) and a web Dashboard to hospitality businesses. Belgium requires every registered cash system to meet the GKS 2.0 standard before it can be used in a venue. Without it, the Belgian market was closed to us.

The work spanned two apps: Merchant, the iPad POS app staff use behind the counter, and the Dashboard, the web app where owners manage their business.
problem:
Fiscal compliance leaves no room for "close enough":

- X and Z reports had to match the FOD specification exactly, down to rounding and grouping
- Every fiscal action needed to be recorded as a signed, tamper-evident event
- Refunds had to work per order line, not just per order
- Cash movements (money in/out) had to be tracked outside of sales
- Staff actions on the device needed to be tied to an identified employee
- Receipts had to carry the required fiscal data

All of this had to land without disrupting existing customers in other countries.
constraints: Report output had to match the FOD specification exactly||Fiscal events must be signed and immutable once recorded||Changes spanned two apps (Merchant and Dashboard) that ship independently||Non-Belgian locations had to keep working unchanged
architecturalDecisions: Fiscal events as the source of truth::Every fiscal action (sale, refund, money in/out) is written as a signed event, and reports are derived from those events::Deriving reports from an immutable event log makes them reproducible and auditable, which is what the regulation asks for.||Refunds per line::Modelled refunds at order-line level instead of reversing whole orders::Partial refunds are common in hospitality, and the fiscal record has to reflect exactly what was returned.||Employee PIN lock on the device::Added a PIN lock to the Merchant iPad app so every fiscal action is tied to a named employee::The standard requires knowing who performed an action, and a PIN is fast enough for staff in a busy venue.||Country-scoped behaviour::Fiscal features activate per location based on country::Keeps the Belgian requirements isolated so other markets are unaffected.
tradeoffs: Exact FOD report format::More rigid report code that is harder to change, in exchange for passing certification||Immutable signed events::Mistakes can only be corrected with new compensating events, never edited
result:
Merchant and the Dashboard now meet GKS 2.0, which opens up the Belgian market for Onesix.

- FOD-exact X/Z reports generated from signed fiscal events
- Per-line refunds, money in/out and fiscal data on receipts
- Employee PIN lock in the Merchant iPad app for traceable staff actions
- Shipped across Merchant and the Dashboard without impacting other markets
diagrams: Fiscal Event Flow::How an order becomes a signed fiscal record and a report::[ Order / Refund / Money in-out ] → [ Signed Fiscal Event ] → [ Receipt with fiscal data ] → [ X/Z Report ]

title: AI and Agents in a Restaurant Dashboard
subtitle: From product image generation to an external MCP server that lets AI agents run a restaurant's back office
summary: Shipped a set of AI features merchants use every day, including image generation, an image-picking assistant, AI start-screen videos and an insights mailbox. Built an external MCP server with OAuth so AI agents can work directly with a merchant's data.
context:
Onesix merchants are restaurant and hospitality owners. They are busy, not designers, and rarely data analysts. Most of the time-consuming work in the Dashboard, our web app for restaurant owners, was content (product photos, Kiosk visuals) and making sense of their numbers.

The goal was to use AI where it removes real work, and to open the platform to the AI agents merchants were starting to use themselves.
problem:
- Good product photos are expensive, and many merchants had none
- Kiosk start screens needed eye-catching visuals that merchants could not produce themselves
- Insights were buried in reports nobody read
- AI agents had no safe way to access a merchant's data
constraints: Features had to work for non-technical merchants with zero setup||Agent access had to be scoped and revocable per merchant||AI output had to fit the existing product and Kiosk data models
architecturalDecisions: AI where the work is::Built image generation and background removal into the Dashboard product editor, plus an assistant that picks matching images from the photo library::Meeting merchants inside the flow they already use beats a separate AI tool they have to discover.||Insights as a mailbox::Delivered AI insights as messages in an inbox instead of another dashboard::Merchants act on short, specific messages, not on charts.||External MCP server with OAuth::Exposed merchant capabilities, including inventory tools, through an MCP server secured with OAuth::MCP lets any agent use the platform, and OAuth gives merchants scoped, revocable consent.||Internal agent platform::Built an internal "Build" platform with remote desktops, agent projects and personas::Running agents in managed environments let the team use them on real work safely.
tradeoffs: Generated product images::Fast and cheap for merchants, but output needs a review step before going live||Open MCP interface::Broader reach for agents, but every exposed tool becomes a public contract to maintain
result:
AI became part of the merchant's daily workflow instead of a demo feature:

- AI product image generation and background removal in the product editor
- An assistant that selects images from the photo library
- AI-generated Kiosk start-screen videos
- An AI insights mailbox
- An external MCP server with OAuth, including inventory tools for agents
diagrams: Agent Access via MCP::How an external AI agent works with a merchant's data::[ AI Agent ] → [ OAuth consent ] → [ Onesix MCP Server ] → [ Products / Inventory / Orders ]

title: Inventory Management for Real Kitchens
subtitle: Modelling recipes, add-ons and sizes so stock levels stay correct with every order
summary: Built inventory management into Merchant, the iPad POS app: stock counts, waste flows, recipe-based deduction that accounts for add-ons and per-size overrides, stock-first screens and bulk entry. Then removed the feature flag and rolled it out to every location.
context: Restaurants lose money on stock they cannot see. Merchants asked for inventory tracking that works with how they actually sell: one product made from several ingredients, sold in different sizes, with add-ons on top.
problem:
- A single order can deduct many ingredients in different amounts
- Add-ons and sizes change how much of each ingredient is used
- Staff need fast flows for counting stock and logging waste
- Large menus make entry one item at a time painfully slow
constraints: Deduction had to be correct for every combination of product, size and add-on||Had to roll out to all existing locations without breaking their order flow||Counting and waste flows had to be quick enough for use during service
architecturalDecisions: Recipe-based deduction::Each product has a recipe, and orders deduct ingredients through it, including add-ons and per-size overrides::Mirrors how kitchens think, so stock levels match reality without manual corrections.||Stock-first screens and bulk entry::Built screens organised around stock items with bulk entry::Setting up a full menu has to take minutes, not days.||Agent tools from day one::Exposed inventory through MCP/agent tools::Lets merchants and agents check and update stock without opening an app.||Flag-gated rollout::Shipped behind a feature flag, then removed the flag once stable::Allowed real-world validation before every location got it.
tradeoffs: Per-size overrides::More configuration surface, but accurate deduction for real menus||Full rollout by removing the flag::Every location gets it, so every edge case becomes a support case
result:
Inventory management is live for every Onesix location:

- Stock counts and waste flows in Merchant
- Recipe deduction including add-ons and per-size overrides
- Stock-first screens and bulk entry for fast setup
- Inventory available to AI agents through MCP tools
- Feature flag removed after a staged rollout
diagrams: Recipe Deduction::How one order line becomes ingredient deductions::[ Order line ] → [ Product recipe ] + [ Size override ] + [ Add-on recipes ] → [ Ingredient deductions ] → [ Stock levels ]

title: Building an AI Service for Application Generation
subtitle: Architecting a scalable backend system to bring AI-powered app generation to a no-code platform
summary: Led the development of a backend Node.js system that handles AI-powered application generation at scale, featuring dynamic prompt engineering, real-time streaming, and micro-frontend architecture.
context:
Betty Blocks is a no-code platform that enables enterprises to build applications without traditional programming. To expand into the AI space, we needed to build a system that could leverage AI to generate full applications—not just code snippets, but complete, functional app components.

This was a greenfield project with high visibility. The challenge was not just making AI work, but making it work reliably at enterprise scale with real-time feedback to users.
problem:
The core technical challenges were interconnected:

- AI responses are slow and unpredictable—users need immediate feedback
- Generated content needs to be transformed into platform-specific formats
- Large data payloads needed to flow between services efficiently
- The frontend needed real-time updates without polling

Beyond the technical aspects, we needed to design a system flexible enough to support multiple AI use cases as the product evolved.
constraints: Real-time user feedback required—no waiting for complete AI responses; Large data transformations needed to happen server-side to protect client performance; System needed to support multiple AI providers and prompt strategies; Integration with existing micro-frontend architecture was mandatory
architecturalDecisions: WebSocket-Based Streaming Architecture::Built a persistent WebSocket connection between frontend and backend for bi-directional real-time communication::HTTP request/response would leave users staring at a loading spinner for 30+ seconds. WebSocket streaming lets us push partial results immediately, showing progress and keeping users engaged.||Dynamic Prompt Engineering Layer::Created an abstraction layer that constructs prompts based on request type, context, and user input::Hardcoded prompts would require code changes for every tweak. A dynamic system lets us iterate on prompt strategies without deployments and A/B test different approaches.||Server-Side Data Transformation Pipeline::All large data transformations happen on the backend before streaming to the client::AI outputs need significant processing to become platform-compatible. Doing this client-side would freeze the UI and expose transformation logic. Server-side keeps clients thin and responsive.||Request Type Router Pattern::Frontend sends a request type identifier, backend routes to appropriate handler with its own prompt strategy and processing pipeline::Keeps the system extensible. Adding new AI features means adding a new handler, not modifying existing code paths.
tradeoffs: WebSocket over Server-Sent Events::More complex connection management and reconnection logic, but enables bi-directional communication for features like cancellation and progress updates.||Centralized backend service over distributed::Single point of failure risk, but simpler to optimize, monitor, and maintain. Added redundancy through proper error handling and graceful degradation.||Dynamic prompts over versioned prompt templates::Harder to reproduce exact behavior for debugging, but allows rapid iteration. Mitigated by logging complete prompts for each request.
result:
The system launched successfully and became a core differentiator for the platform:

- Real-time streaming reduced perceived wait times by 80%
- Modular architecture enabled 5 new AI features in the following quarter
- Backend handles thousands of concurrent AI sessions
- Zero client performance degradation despite large data payloads

The project demonstrated that AI integration is as much about user experience and architecture as it is about the AI itself.
diagrams: System Architecture::Request flow from frontend through WebSocket to AI service and back::[ Frontend ] ←WebSocket→ [ Node.js Service ] ←HTTP→ [ AI Provider ] → [ Transform ] → [ Stream to Client ]

title: Building a Fast and Scalable Component Tree
subtitle: Replacing a buggy tree view with a high-performance solution using React optimization patterns
summary: Identified performance issues in the platform's page builder tree view and took initiative to build a proof-of-concept that became the production solution—faster, more reliable, and scalable to thousands of components.
context:
The Betty Blocks page builder is a visual editor where users construct application pages by arranging components in a hierarchical structure. This structure is displayed as a tree view that users interact with constantly—selecting, reordering, nesting, and editing components.

The existing tree implementation had accumulated technical debt. It was slow with large component counts, had subtle bugs with drag-and-drop, and the codebase had become difficult to maintain.
problem:
The tree view had multiple interconnected issues:

- Performance degraded significantly beyond 200 components
- Re-renders cascaded through the entire tree on any change
- Drag-and-drop had edge cases that caused incorrect nesting
- State management was scattered and hard to reason about

Previous attempts to fix these issues had added complexity without solving the root causes. The codebase needed a fresh approach, not more patches.
constraints: Must support trees with 1000+ components without lag; Feature parity with existing implementation required; Could not disrupt ongoing feature development—needed to be a clean swap; Had to prove the concept before getting buy-in for full implementation
architecturalDecisions: Proof-of-Concept First Approach::Built a working PoC on my own initiative before proposing the rewrite to stakeholders::Proposals for rewrites often get rejected because the risk is unclear. A working demo shows exactly what's possible and de-risks the decision for stakeholders.||Aggressive Memoization Strategy::Used useMemo and useCallback extensively to prevent unnecessary re-renders::Tree structures are worst-case for React rendering—a change at any level can trigger re-renders all the way down. Memoization breaks this cascade by ensuring stable references.||Virtualized Rendering for Large Trees::Only render visible tree nodes, with buffer zones for smooth scrolling::With 1000+ components, rendering everything to the DOM is wasteful. Virtualization keeps the DOM small regardless of data size.||Normalized State Structure::Stored tree data in a flat normalized structure with parent references rather than deeply nested objects::Deeply nested state is hard to update immutably and causes reference changes to cascade. Normalized data enables surgical updates to individual nodes.
tradeoffs: Full rewrite over incremental refactor::Higher upfront investment, but the existing code's architecture made incremental fixes ineffective. Clean slate enabled proper patterns from the start.||Heavy memoization over simpler code::Added complexity to component logic, but performance requirements made this necessary. Documented patterns clearly for team understanding.||Custom virtualization over library::More implementation work, but tree virtualization has specific requirements (variable heights, nested expansion) that generic libraries handle poorly.
result:
The new tree view shipped and immediately improved the page builder experience:

- Renders 1000+ components at 60fps (previous implementation stuttered at 200)
- Eliminated all known drag-and-drop bugs
- Reduced tree-related bug reports by 90%
- Codebase is now maintainable and well-documented

The project also demonstrated the value of developer initiative—identifying problems and proposing solutions rather than waiting for tickets.
diagrams: Render Optimization Flow::How memoization prevents cascade re-renders in the tree structure::[ Parent Change ] → [ Stable Callbacks ] → [ memo() Check ] → [ Skip Child Re-render ]

title: Helping Development Teams Perform
subtitle: Identifying team bottlenecks and implementing alignment practices that improved collaboration
summary: Observed misalignment and communication gaps in a development team, then implemented bi-weekly alignment sessions that transformed team dynamics and delivery.
context:
I've worked across multiple development teams at Betty Blocks, and in each one I pay attention to what's holding the team back. Technical problems are often symptoms of people problems—miscommunication, unclear goals, or siloed knowledge.

In one team, I noticed a pattern: developers were working hard but often in slightly different directions. People didn't know what others were working on, and there was no shared understanding of the bigger picture we were building toward.
problem:
The symptoms were subtle but impactful:

- Duplicate work when two devs unknowingly tackled related problems
- Integration conflicts because approaches weren't aligned early
- Hesitancy to ask questions or raise concerns
- Sprint goals achieved but overall progress felt slow

This wasn't a hostile or dysfunctional team—just a quiet one. People were heads-down on their tasks without enough moments to surface and align.
constraints: Could not mandate large process changes—needed voluntary participation; Had to respect existing sprint ceremonies and not add meeting fatigue; Needed to create safety for people to speak up without forcing it; Changes had to show results quickly to maintain buy-in
architecturalDecisions: Bi-Weekly Developer Alignment Sessions::Established a regular 30-minute session just for developers, no managers, focused on alignment rather than status::Standups are too brief for real discussion. Retrospectives happen too infrequently. A dedicated developer-only space encourages honest conversation about technical direction.||Open Question Format::Instead of status updates, asked each developer if they had questions or concerns about what we're building as a team::Status updates encourage "everything is fine" responses. Questions encourage curiosity and surface hidden confusion or disagreement.||Voluntary Facilitation Rotation::Rotated who led the session to distribute ownership::If one person always runs it, it becomes "their meeting." Rotation made it truly a team practice.
tradeoffs: Informal sessions over structured agile ceremony::Less measurable and documented, but lower friction and more likely to get honest participation.||Developer-only over whole team::Excludes valuable stakeholder perspectives, but creates psychological safety for technical disagreements and questions.||Bi-weekly over weekly::Less frequent touchpoints, but respects team's time and keeps sessions from feeling like overhead.
result:
The impact went beyond the sessions themselves:

- Developers started collaborating outside of scheduled meetings
- Technical decisions were discussed earlier, reducing integration issues
- New team members ramped up faster with better context sharing
- Team velocity increased as duplicated effort decreased

The biggest win was cultural: people felt more connected to each other and to the team's mission. Technical excellence comes from teams that communicate well.
diagrams: Before and After Team Dynamics::How communication patterns changed with alignment sessions::[ Before: Siloed Work ] → [ Alignment Sessions ] → [ After: Connected Collaboration ]
